slides.title: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)
slides.prompt: RAII is a core C++ programming idiom where resource life cycle (memory, file handles, sockets) is bound to object lifetime. Resources are acquired in constructors and released automatically in destructors.

slides.title: Automatic Cleanup with Destructor
slides.prompt: Fill in the special member function signature that releases resources when an object goes out of scope.

slides.title: Primary Advantage of RAII
slides.prompt: What is the primary benefit of adhering to the RAII pattern in C++?
options: Guarantees exception-safe resource release and prevents leaks when functions exit early
Eliminates the need for class constructors entirely
Replaces static memory allocation with heap memory
slides.correctAnswer: Guarantees exception-safe resource release and prevents leaks when functions exit early

slides.title: Heap Allocation operator
slides.prompt: Fill in the operator used to dynamically allocate memory on the heap.

slides.title: Raw Pointer Risks
slides.prompt: Which issue commonly arises when managing memory manually with raw pointers using new/delete?
options: Memory leaks, double deletion, and dangling pointers
Stack overflow errors on small objects
slides.correctAnswer: Memory leaks, double deletion, and dangling pointers

slides.title: Heap Deallocation
slides.prompt: Fill in the keyword used to free memory previously allocated with new[].
slides.codeSnippet:
int* arr = new int[50];
___[] arr; // Deallocates heap array

slides.title: Stack vs Heap Allocation
slides.prompt: What happens to variables allocated directly on the stack when their enclosing scope ends?
options: They are popped off the stack and destroyed automatically
They remain in memory until explicit delete is called
They are converted into heap allocations
They cause dangling reference errors automatically
slides.correctAnswer: They are popped off the stack and destroyed automatically
